title: Introduction
description: Five quick questions on GTO vs. exploit and notation. Get all five right before moving to Part 1.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes Game Theory Optimal (GTO) play?

choices.text: A strategy that maximally exploits any opponent.
A mixed strategy that is unexploitable in theory — the Nash equilibrium of the game.
The strategy used by the player with the largest stack.
A strategy that always folds to large bets.

questions.explanation: GTO is the Nash equilibrium: a mixed strategy such that no opponent can win money against it in expectation. Crucially, it is defensive — it does not maximally exploit known leaks.

questions.prompt: At microstakes the population systematically deviates from GTO. Which set of deviations is most accurate?

choices.text: Bluffs and calls at exactly the GTO frequency.
Plays randomly with no statistical bias.

questions.explanation: The microstakes population over-calls (especially on the river) and under-bluffs. The correct exploit is to value-bet more and bluff less than GTO would suggest.

questions.prompt: Which set of hands does `A2s+` represent?

choices.text: All suited aces from A2s through AKs.
All offsuit aces from A2 through AK.
All hands containing at least one ace.

questions.explanation: `A2s+` denotes the suited-ace block from A2s up to AKs — twelve hands total.

questions.prompt: If a strategy is unexploitable (GTO), it is also the highest-EV strategy against any specific opponent.
questions.explanation: Unexploitability ≠ maximum EV. GTO is a defensive baseline; against a known-leaky opponent, deliberate exploitative deviation extracts more EV.

questions.prompt: Which of the following symbols are defined in the curriculum's notation table?

choices.text: P — pot before the current bet

questions.explanation: P, B, n, and SPR are all defined. There is no curriculum-wide K symbol — kicker strength is informal.
